nameStory: The Greater Anglewing gets its name from the distinctive angular, diamond-shaped wings that set it apart from other katydids. The 'greater' part distinguishes it from its smaller cousin, the Lesser Anglewing, making it the big sibling of the angle-winged katydid family.
description: The Greater Anglewing is a large, leaf-green katydid that's perfectly disguised as foliage. These impressive insects grow 2-2.6 inches long, making them among the bigger katydids you'll encounter in New England. Their most striking feature is their rhombus or diamond-shaped wings that give them an angular appearance quite different from typical katydids. Like living leaves, they blend seamlessly into the trees and shrubs where they spend their lives.

idTips.label: Diamond-shaped wings
idTips.description: The wings form a distinctive angular, rhombus shape rather than the oval wings of most katydids - run your eye along the wing edge to trace the geometric diamond pattern

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably bigger than most katydids at over 2 inches long - about the size of your thumb from tip to first joint

idTips.label: Leaf-green coloration
idTips.description: Bright to medium green color that perfectly matches fresh leaves, sometimes with subtle yellow-green tones that mimic leaf veins

idTips.label: Ticking call
idTips.description: Males produce a distinctive 'tick-tick-tick' sound rather than the typical katydid 'katy-did' call - sounds like a quiet clock ticking in the trees

idTips.label: Tree-dwelling behavior
idTips.description: Found high up in tree canopies and shrubs rather than on the ground, often remaining motionless during the day like a perfectly still leaf

habitat: Greater Anglewings live in the canopies of deciduous trees and tall shrubs throughout New England's forests, parks, and wooded neighborhoods. They particularly favor oak, maple, and other broad-leafed trees where their leaf mimicry works best. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations, anywhere there's sufficient tree cover to support their arboreal lifestyle.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not present - eggs are overwintering and nymphs haven't yet developed.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs may be present but are rarely seen due to their excellent camouflage and small size in early stages.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity time when adults emerge and are most visible and vocal, making their distinctive ticking calls from late August through October.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, leaving only eggs to survive the winter months.

funFact: Greater Anglewings are such convincing leaf mimics that they even sway gently in the breeze like real leaves, and some individuals have wing patterns that look exactly like leaf damage, complete with fake 'holes' and 'brown spots' to sell the disguise!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Lesser Anglewing, but the Greater is noticeably larger and has more pronounced angular wing edges. Memory trick: 'Greater' means bigger and more angular - if it looks like a big green diamond with legs, you've found the Greater!
compareHints: The Greater Anglewing is significantly larger than its relative the Lesser Anglewing and has more dramatically angled, diamond-shaped wings. While both species are green leaf mimics, the Greater's wings have sharper, more pronounced angles that create a more geometric appearance. The Lesser Anglewing has more gently curved wing edges and a smaller overall body size.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Lesser Anglewing is smaller and more delicate than its close relative the Greater Anglewing, with proportionally narrower wings and a more slender build.
